claims.text: An equimolar WTaCrV alloy is an example of the proposed W-based refractory HEA intermediate layer.
Conventional processing can produce this W-based HEA with a homogeneous microstructure suitable for use between tungsten and a heat sink.
A controlled post-fabrication anneal can induce stepwise, coherent nanoprecipitation in the HEA matrix.
The annealing temperature and duration can be selected within a microstructural stability window that permits nanoprecipitation without melting or dissolving the matrix.
Refractory HEA interlayers are relevant to plasma-facing components operating under high thermal flux and irradiation exposure.
The anneal will produce coherent nanoprecipitates with well-bonded interfaces in the HEA matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitates will act as conduits for heat transfer by reducing phonon scattering at grain boundaries.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve residual thermal stresses.
Coherent interfaces inhibit damaging microcrack formation by reducing stress concentrations associated with crack initiation.
The nanoprecipitate-mediated effects will enhance the effective thermal conductivity of the intermediate layer.
The coherent nanoprecipitates will maintain mechanical stability under cyclic thermal and irradiation loading.
The annealed HEA will have higher effective thermal conductivity than the untreated HEA.
The annealed HEA will preserve or improve strength and ductility under high-temperature conditions.
The annealed HEA will preserve or improve strength and ductility under irradiation.
The as-fabricated HEA interlayer meets minimum structural-integrity requirements but has lower heat-transfer performance than the targeted annealed material.
The heat-transfer and structural benefits will persist across typical plasma-facing-component temperatures and irradiation loads if the microstructure remains stable.
The magnitude of any conductivity improvement depends on nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and coherency.
Nanoprecipitates may also introduce phonon-scattering effects that offset their proposed thermal-conduction benefit.
A controlled comparison of annealed and as-fabricated samples can test conductivity, mechanical integrity, and nanoprecipitate formation under simulated service conditions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant conductivity increase, or observation of degraded mechanical integrity, would refute the hypothesis.
